extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics, mathematicians and computer scientists interested in computational methods, formal verification, and mathematical epistemology
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for assessing the use of computers in mathematical research — both as tools for discovery (experimentation, simulation, pattern-finding) and as tools for justification (probabilistic tests, brute-force enumeration, formal verification) — and for assessing what counts as mathematical understanding. Targets philosophical and practical evaluation of computational methods in mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computation for gaining insight and intuition
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of computations to gain insight and intuition about mathematical objects, phenomena, or conjectures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: running examples, numerical evaluation, plotting/graphical displays. Anti-pattern: large-scale output (e.g., printout of many primes) that yields no conceptual understanding. Emphasizes that what mathematicians want is understanding, not mere collections of answers (Thurston quote).

rubrics_metrics.name: Computation for discovering new patterns and relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: Using computation to discover patterns, regularities, or relationships that suggest new conjectures or definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: searching integer-sequence databases (OEIS), using inverse symbolic calculators to recognize closed forms. Guidance: computations can suggest conjectures but do not by themselves provide deductive warrant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of graphical displays to suggest underlying principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Using graphical representations to reveal structure, guide intuition, and suggest mathematical principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: visualizing dynamical systems or complex objects; visual tools that make properties apparent. Success measured by whether visualization leads to tractable hypotheses or explanations (see Mancosu, 2005).

rubrics_metrics.name: Computation for testing and falsifying conjectures
rubrics_metrics.description: Using computation to test conjectures on many cases and to potentially falsify them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: brute-force counterexample search, large-scale enumeration. Role: discovery-side tool to show conjectures fail or hold in many cases; does not replace a proof but can guide refinement or abandonment of conjectures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploratory computation to assess whether results merit formal proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Using computational exploration to decide whether a putative result is worth investing effort for a formal proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: exploratory runs, heuristic searches, or simulations used to focus research effort; pragmatic criterion for allocating finite research resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computation to suggest approaches for formal proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Using computational experiments and patterns to generate plausible proof strategies or lemmas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: patterns discovered computationally that indicate invariants or structural decompositions which become the seeds of formal proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer-based derivations replacing lengthy hand calculations
rubrics_metrics.description: Using computer algebra systems or automated routines to perform lengthy or error-prone derivations that would otherwise be done by hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Mathematica or Maple simplifying complex expressions. Guidance: helpful for reducing human error and freeing attention for conceptual issues; must be reproducible and documented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computation for confirming analytically derived results
rubrics_metrics.description: Using computational checks to confirm results obtained by analytic reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: numeric evaluation of formulas, cross-checking symbolic manipulations. Provides secondary assurance but not a substitute for proof; increases confidence when independent methods agree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between discovery and justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate the role of computation in formulating definitions/conjectures (discovery) versus providing warrant that claims are true (justification).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: many computational activities blur the line (simulations that yield important results without formal hypotheses). Evaluation should treat discovery- and justification-oriented uses differently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof-as-deductive-warrant (traditional standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: The proper warrant for a mathematical theorem is a deductive proof using valid inferences from accepted axioms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: this is the traditional benchmark for truth. Discussions of computational methods should situate themselves relative to this ideal (e.g., ask when an ordinary/computational proof indicates the existence of a formal one).

rubrics_metrics.name: Surveyability/surveyability of proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an informal or computational proof is presented in a way that indicates (and allows a competent mathematician to see) the existence of a formal, gapless derivation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors: size/complexity of inferential steps, implicit background knowledge, and whether inferential rules are spelled out. Lack of surveyability reduces the degree of warranted acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degrees of faith based on theorem/proof features
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptance of a proof may vary in degree depending on theorem complexity, proof complexity, computational methods used, and reliability/authority of the authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: mathematicians often express varying confidence (degrees of faith); computational or lengthy proofs may warrant lower intuitive confidence unless corroborated or formalized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probabilistic computational evidence (e.g., probabilistic primality tests)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of probabilistic algorithms/tests that make conclusions 'virtually certain' (e.g., Solovay–Strassen, Rabin–Miller) as inductive evidence for mathematical claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: such tests yield very high confidence but not certainty; their epistemic role should be evaluated in terms of reliability, error rates, and the decision-theoretic context in which one acts on their output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal verification as near-absolute certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of proof assistants and formalization to provide near-absolute assurance that a theorem has a correct proof (e.g., projects verifying prime number theorem, four-color theorem, Kepler conjecture).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: formal verification currently costly; where applied, it provides strong warrant. Evaluation should weigh the cost/benefit: does the near-certainty justify the effort?

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility and checkability of computational proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Computational proofs should be reproducible (code/data available) and, where possible, yield justifications checkable by hand or independent methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: McCune's EQP produced checkable output; Appel–Haken and Hales produced extensive computational data. Anti-pattern: opaque, unpublished code or data that prevents independent verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction to combinatorial enumeration and numerical bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: A common pattern: reduce a proof to a finite (but large) combinatorial enumeration and numerical/optimization bounds solvable by computation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: four-color theorem, Kepler conjecture. Evaluation: scrutinize the reduction's correctness, completeness of enumeration, and numerical stability of bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability judged by past performance and system design
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessing the trustworthiness of computational methods by empirical measures of reliability (e.g., 'five-nines' uptime analogy) and by understanding system design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: pragmatic confidence may rest more on past performance and engineering understanding than on elaborate philosophical modeling. But past performance is only an imperfect indicator.

rubrics_metrics.name: The need for a modeled space of possibilities when assigning probabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Assigning probabilities to mathematical assertions requires specifying an appropriate space of possibilities or distributions over types of calculations/instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: philosophical attempts (Gaifman, Hacking, Good) wrestle with how to model such spaces; without them, probability assignments risk being arbitrary. Practical approach: model the distribution of relevant problem instances in the domain of application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local coherence and bounded deductive powers (Gaifman)
rubrics_metrics.description: Allowing probability assignments to be coherent relative to the deductive consequences an agent can actually see, given bounded resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: supports 'local' rational acceptance of computational test results; still requires scrutiny whether this adds normative force beyond showing a procedure is usually reliable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commitment vs performance distinction (Levi)
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate between ideal commitments of a rational agent (what they ought to be committed to deductively) and actual performance given bounded reasoning resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: normative accounts (commitment) differ from practical decision procedures (performance); evaluating computational methods should consider both aspects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design of useful procedures for bounded agents (minimize errors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Development and evaluation of procedures (algorithms, tests, heuristics) that, given resource bounds, provide correct judgments most of the time and minimize errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: theoretical computer science provides models (complexity, probabilistic guarantees). Practical assessment: does a procedure have provable performance guarantees appropriate to the task?

rubrics_metrics.name: The role of explanation and understanding beyond correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluations should include whether a proof or computational result provides explanation, conceptual insight, analogies, or improved representations — not just truth-warrant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: new proofs can be important for the insight they provide even when prior proofs were correct. Negative judgment: computationally intensive proofs sometimes fail to deliver the desired insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical theories must be context-sensitive and practically useful
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophical accounts of mathematical evidence and understanding should be tied to specific mathematical and scientific contexts and further inquiry, not studied in isolation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: success criteria include helping design computational systems, clarifying informal data they are meant to explain, and providing concrete standards (e.g., verifying inferences, designing informative visualizations).
